Established the CalFUSE roadmap for load flexibility, established new principles for electric rates and demand flexibility, authorized two working groups, and expanded the PG&E and SCE dynamic pricing pilots from Decision 21-12-015. 5 1.3 Overview of this study The California Price Response Potential Study report proceeds as follows. The second section of the report describes the study’s methodology, with subsections on baseline load data, dynamic price profiles, end use load responses, technology cost characterization, and metrics for quantifying the impacts of price response. The third section presents results, as grouped by price profiles, end use load response, technical potential, economic potential, and battery storage system value proposition. The fourth section presents a far-ranging discussion, encompassing the topics of non-marginal changes to system load, evaluation of tariff design scenarios, behavioral considerations, price response across end uses, behind the meter storage considerations, and limitations/future work. 2 Methodology This study models the load impacts, customer costs, and system impacts of key end uses as they respond to hourly prices in 2019 and 2030 using automation technology. A set of new end use response models (described in Section 2.3) were developed for this study that estimate the behavior of automated load response algorithms, based on a given baseline end use load profile and a given price profile. The baseline end use load profiles (Section 2.1) come from an existing set of load shapes that represent the entire California IOU territory for clusters of customers at the end use level. Battery energy storage systems are also considered; we assess the value proposition of these systems responding to the various price profiles explored in this study.
